Telegram Channels vs Groups vs Bots: The Difference That Actually Matters
Telegram has three kinds of “places”, and content creators mix them up constantly. Here is the mental model that sticks.
A channel is a megaphone
One-way broadcasting: admins post, subscribers read. No reply threads by default (though a discussion group can be attached), unlimited subscribers, and posts carry the
channel's
name — or the name of the posting bot if “Sign messages with a bot” is on. Channels are where scheduled content lives.
A group is a campfire

Everyone talks. Groups are for community; up to 200k members in supergroups, full message history, topics if enabled. You do not “schedule to a group” the way you do to a channel — that is what channels are for.
A bot is a worker
Bots are accounts run by software. In your channel's context, a bot is the
hands
that type the message: a bot must be an admin with
for anything to be published. That is exactly why Fast Scheduler pairs a sender bot with your channel — your bot posts, under your brand.
Why this matters for scheduling
Want posts to appear at fixed times?
Channel + scheduler + sender bot.
Want subscribers to discuss the posts? Attach a
linked discussion group
to the channel — comments live there automatically.
Want automation, menus, and commands? That is the
bot
layer — the part Fast Scheduler turns into a full publishing workflow.
One nuance worth knowing: Telegram shows
signed
posts as “via bot” only when the admin chooses to sign with the bot; otherwise the post simply appears under the channel name. Either way, the sender bot did the typing.
Common questions
Can a scheduled post go to a group?
Fast Scheduler targets channels (including chat-announcement channels). Groups are conversational — schedule announcements to a channel instead.
Do subscribers see which bot posted?
By default a channel post shows just the channel name. If the channel enables signing posts with the admin bot, the sender bot is credited.
